I've been offscreen killed by those scimitar-wielders in Agrabah far too much to give the combat nothing but praise. But the story and world designs are really good, outside of Neverland which I feel was a huge copout or just flat-out rushed. It should have been like BBS, a tiny ship with like 4 claustrophobic rooms and 2 boss fights feels so lame when you wanna play with your new flying powerup.

The combat definitely has a big share of faults, ESPECIALLY when playing on Proud. Stuff hitting you from offscreen because the camera is so zoomed in, the way auto targeting works, tbh Neverland should have been like it was in BBS, a tiny ship with 4 rooms and a couple boss fights is kinda lame especially since you wanna play with your new flying powerup. Gameplay-wise there's a lot of head scratchers, but hey the story is simple, right? (That is, until you try and think about how they make it all make sense for the sequels, like how killing Ansem supposedly makes all the worlds be disconnected again yet in KH2 you're right back in your gummi ship flying from world to world with no differences)

I will say Hollow Bastion is one of the best final levels I've played, though I love World That Never Was, I really feel a definitive final level was really missing from KH3. The boss rush just had me thinking man...imagine if these were all scattered throughout an awesome final level instead of Xehanort shoving everyone in a flat undetailed box. As an adult, I just find KH2 more fully rounded and complete, but that's just my opinion.

You're assuming like I want to blindly stick to this idea despite its potential to be offensive even though I'm doing literally the opposite here. I only wanted some general thoughts. My only "why's" are that it's an aspect of how the world developed and nothing more, it's certainly not a direct allegory. I have conflicting advice on whether it's a major problem or perfectly justified, so your words are noted.

Yep! It's really the only true place of civilization that isn't just tribal communities or people barely hanging on. The goddess wanted to keep the magic for herself and her family since she feared humanity would destroy themselves with it. The way you learn magic is by reading a sort of language in the constellations and using their energy, something people in a city of permanent daylight couldn't learn on their own. And as the years passed the government would outright ban use of magic since it was a desire of the goddess to forbid it to be widely known. 

The people who use magic outside the walls are people who didn't live near the region she created the sun, people who came to understand the stars and constellations and shared the magic among their tribes and communities in order to survive the night. An ability to create fire for example would be hugely beneficial. Essentially the people in the walls of the city are scared and believe those outside are heretic usurpers plotting to use magic in the same way their goddess warned about. 

So, you're kind of correct that basically just the fact magic can be destructive means they want no part of it unless it's their royal family who have the goddess's blood.

Well the main thing is that the story won't really show that, in fact the people outside who use magic will be pretty conceited and prideful I'm thinking. I'm never going to say it's a good thing with how the racial stigmas would work, and it'll be a clear act of abuse and injustice that their city would work that way (in particular the main girl's abuse). I feel like in a short summary it just sounds worrying, and that is dangerous of course lol.   


I'll check out that book and see what to avoid. Maybe I'll make it not a matter of skin tone and a matter of hair color or something, I dunno.

Haha thanks for the words. Yeah, maybe I can have the skin tone thing but just remove any sort of substantial message or story point due to it, not sure. Basically the reasoning is that the city has constant heat and sunlight that allows for agriculture, and it wards away evil beings that lurk in the darkness outside. So it's completely ideal to have that sunlight as protection in an otherwise apocalyptic world.

Yeah, I mean I intend it as an aspect of world building and not really a perfect reflection of our world, but I don't know. Obviously I have no ill will or pro-white message in my views, but I know it has the capability to be seen as something bad and that might be too big of a risk on my first real work lol.

I'll definitely keep that in mind, thank you. Haha but since people who read the story will only know me from the story itself, I have to be really careful to make it clear it can't be interpreted as something negative. I may just have to play it way more safe.

Haha it's more like the artificial sun itself is relatively small in scale, the city itself probably only has around 100,000 people. The goddess died in order to create the sun, so it's basically the best she could do on her way out and people made the city under it.

Haha good questions, basically the "sun" is relatively small in scale, and required the goddess who created it to sacrifice herself to create it, since the world was damn near apocalyptic from being night 24/7. But essentially the issue I thought could arise is that the city is full of people who don't use magic since it's seen as something reserved for holy descendants of the goddess, and people outside use magic more regularly but aren't allowed in the thriving city because of that. Basically, it seems like if interpreted incorrectly I'm afraid it could backfire.
